title: 92% of Bangladesh's energy climate finance came as loans: study
excerpt: Of $2.54 billion traced between 2002 and 2023, only $203 million was grants, Change Initiative found, as Bangladesh presses for grants at COP31.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: rooftop solar panels on a village house, with a gas power plant beyond the paddy fields

content:
About 92% of the climate finance Bangladesh’s energy sector received between 2002 and 2023 came as loans, a study by the Dhaka think tank Change Initiative has found. Of about US$2.54 billion in identified finance, roughly $2.34 billion was loans and $203 million grants, The Daily Star reported on 10 November.

The study was presented on 3 November at a national dialogue on debt sustainability in the energy sector, held at CIRDAP in Dhaka, The Business Standard reported.

Main findings

  • Bangladesh received about nine dollars in loans for every dollar in grants for energy-sector climate finance.
  • It borrows the equivalent of $29.52 for each tonne of its annual carbon dioxide emissions, close to the least developed country average of $30.49, The Daily Star reported.
  • Bangladesh emitted about 108 million tonnes of CO2 in 2024, around 0.24% of the world total, according to figures cited in the coverage.
  • More than 60% of power generation depends on imported fuels, The Business Standard reported from the dialogue.

What the study recommends

  • More grant-based finance and more affordable loans in local currency.
  • At least 1.5% of total bank lending directed to renewable energy, and a green finance target of 15% to 20% by 2030.
  • Pooling small rooftop solar projects, and letting private investors install solar on factory roofs and sell power to the factories.
  • Credit for the roughly 8,500 smaller renewable energy service providers, with government quality checks.
  • Raising loss and damage at COP31 together with other Global South countries.

Change Initiative chief executive M Zakir Hossain Khan urged developing countries to push for unconditional grants, debt relief linked to climate impacts and clearer climate finance accounting, The Daily Star reported. Environment minister Abdul Awal Mintoo told the newspaper Bangladesh would seek grant-based finance and loss and damage support at the summit.

Why it matters

The finding adds to the case Bangladesh is making at COP31, which opened in Antalya on 9 November, that climate support should come as grants. For NGOs and donors, it is a reminder that much of what is counted as climate finance adds to national debt. A November 2025 Change Initiative index, which Devlens covered at the start of the summit, reached a similar conclusion across all climate finance.

Limitations

The report itself has not been published online, so Devlens could not check the method or the list of projects. “Identified” finance means only what the authors could trace. Counting loans for coal and gas plants as climate finance is contested, and the figures should not be read as Bangladesh’s total climate finance.

What to watch

  • Whether Bangladesh’s COP31 delegation sets a figure for grant-based adaptation or loss and damage finance before the summit ends on 20 November.
  • Publication of the full study by Change Initiative.
